cards.prompt:
Apps send data in one of two ways. **TCP** is like a tracked parcel: the sender finds out whether it arrived, lost pieces are sent again, and everything is put back in order. **UDP** is like a postcard: quick, but nobody checks that it arrived, and a lost one is never sent again.

Which way suits each job?

items.label: Sending a photo in a chat
Saving a document to the cloud
Your car's position in a racing game

cards.explanation: A download, an email, a photo or a saved document is broken if a single piece is missing, so they use **TCP**. Live calls, voice chat and game positions are about **right now**: a lost moment is soon replaced by a newer one, so waiting for it would only cause lag. They usually use **UDP**.
cards.hint: For each job, ask: would one missing piece ruin it? Or is it live, so old data is useless by the time it could be sent again?
cards.nudge: Look at the live jobs again. By the time a lost piece of a call or a game could be sent again, a newer one has already replaced it.

cards.title: Reliable or fast
cards.body:
**TCP** (Transmission Control [[Protocol]]) is the tracked parcel. It sets up a connection first, numbers the pieces so they go back in order, and resends anything lost.

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is the postcard: no setup, no checking that it arrived. Quick, but lost data stays lost.

Both travel inside IP [[packets|packet]], and both use **ports**.

cards.prompt: Before TCP sends any data, both sides check they can hear each other, using three short messages. This is the **three-way handshake**. Put the start of a connection in order.

items.label: Server: "Yes! Can you hear me too?" (SYN-ACK)
Browser sends its request for the web page

cards.explanation: The browser asks (**SYN**, short for *synchronise*), the server agrees and checks back (**SYN-ACK**), and the browser confirms (**ACK**, *acknowledge*). Only then is the connection open, so the request comes last.
cards.hint: Each message answers the one before it. And no data is sent until all three handshake messages are done.
cards.nudge: The request can't go until the handshake is finished. Which message starts a conversation, and which one replies to a question?

cards.prompt: You're on a video call and one [[packet]] of video goes missing. Imagine the call used **TCP**. What would happen?

options.text: The picture freezes until the lost piece is resent, then jumps ahead
The call skips the lost piece straight away and carries on smoothly
options.nudge: Skipping lost data is what a postcard does. TCP is the tracked parcel: what does it insist on before moving on?

options.text: The call ends, because TCP can't carry on with a missing piece
options.nudge: TCP doesn't give up after one lost piece. Think about what it does with anything that goes missing.

options.text: The call quietly switches to UDP for the rest of the conversation
options.nudge: TCP never turns itself into a different protocol. It has its own way of dealing with a lost piece.

cards.explanation: TCP waits for the lost piece to be **sent again** and keeps everything in order, so the picture would freeze, then rush to catch up. That's why calls usually use **UDP**: a face frozen mid-sneeze for a split second beats the whole call stopping to wait.
cards.hint: TCP resends anything lost and keeps the pieces in order. What does the video have to do while it waits for the missing piece?

cards.prompt: Match each activity to the reason it's delivered that way.

pairs.right: Every piece must arrive, in order

pairs.left: Voice chat in a game (usually UDP)
pairs.right: Fresh sound matters more than late sound
One tiny question and answer, so skip the setup

cards.explanation: A download is useless with a single piece missing, so it uses **TCP**. Voice chat would rather skip a lost moment than stall waiting for it, so it usually uses **UDP**. A DNS lookup is one small question, so a handshake would take longer than the question itself: it usually uses **UDP**, and switches to TCP for large answers.
cards.hint: Ask of each one: would it be ruined by one missing piece, would it rather skip old data, or is it too small to be worth a setup?
cards.nudge: Think tracked parcel vs postcard. A file needs every piece; live sound can't wait for late data; a tiny question isn't worth a [[handshake]].

options.text: It sends without a handshake and doesn't resend lost data
It doesn't resend lost data, but it always delivers in order
options.nudge: Putting data back in order is one of TCP's jobs. UDP makes no promises, so data can arrive jumbled.

options.text: Its data travels on its own, without going inside IP packets
options.nudge: Both TCP and UDP travel inside IP packets. IP gets the data to the right computer either way.

options.text: It skips port numbers, so it only works for one program at a time
options.nudge: Both TCP and UDP need to reach the right program on a computer. What does that job?

cards.explanation: UDP has **no handshake** and **no resending**. It doesn't guarantee order either: data can arrive jumbled. Like [[TCP]], it travels inside IP packets and uses ports. A [[DNS]] lookup is a common UDP example.
cards.hint: UDP is the postcard: no setup, no checking that it arrived, it just sends. Which statement fits that and nothing more?

cards.prompt: Your browser sends a SYN ("Can we talk?") and the server replies with a SYN-ACK, but the SYN-ACK is **lost** on the way. What happens?

options.text: Both sides wait, then resend their message
The connection opens anyway, because the server received the SYN
options.nudge: The connection needs all three steps, not just the first one. The browser never heard back, so it isn't finished yet.

options.text: The browser starts sending data without finishing the handshake
options.nudge: TCP never sends data before the handshake is complete. Think about what a side does when a reply doesn't come.

options.text: The browser automatically switches to UDP instead
options.nudge: TCP doesn't change into a different protocol on its own. It has its own way of dealing with lost messages.

cards.explanation:
Both sides are waiting. The browser never got a SYN-ACK, so after a short wait it **sends its SYN again**. The server never got an ACK, so it **sends its SYN-ACK again**. Once a SYN-ACK gets through and the ACK comes back, the connection opens. If nothing gets through after several tries, the browser gives up and shows an error.

The connection can't open without all three steps, [[TCP]] never sends data before the handshake finishes, and it doesn't switch to UDP.
cards.hint: The connection only opens after all three messages arrive. If one goes missing, what is each side still waiting for?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **TCP**: a handshake first, numbered pieces, and resending anything lost.
- **UDP**: no handshake, no resending; quick, but lost data stays lost.
- Files and email need TCP; live calls and games prefer UDP.

Next: the rules on top, like [[HTTP]], DNS and email.
